newsitem.title: USA: Jury to consider sentence for sergeant in rapes. [CORRECTED 18:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Jury to consider sentence for sergeant in rapes. [CORRECTED 18:55 GMT]

text.p: A military jury begins deliberations Monday on whether a Army drill sergeant should receive life in prison for raping six (corrects from 18) female trainees at the Aberdeen Proving Ground.
The jury on April 29 found Army Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson guilty of 18 counts of rape in the most prominent case of a sexual misconduct scandal at the Proving Ground.

Simpson was acquitted of one additional rape count but found guilty of indecent assault. He also was found guilty of 25 of 35 other sexual misconduct counts against him, not guilty of seven and guilty of lesser offences on three.

Simpson, 32, could face life in prison for the rape convictions. He already had pleaded guilty to 11 counts of consensual sex and five counts of propositioning, for which he faced a maximum sentence of 32 years in prison.
The sentencing deliberations were scheduled to begin on Monday morning, but were postponed until 7 p.m. EDT so that the six-member court-martial panel could hear from a character witness for Simpson.
Army Trial Judge Col. Paul Johnston has ordered a gag rule on counsel until after the sentencing hearing.
If Simpson is sentenced to more than a year in jail or dismissed from the service for bad conduct, the case would automatically go to the Army's Court of Criminal Appeals.

If the Army court of appeals upholds the verdict, then Simpson could appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces. If that court does not take the case, then Simpson could go to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Simpson was the first of 12 trainers charged with various acts of misconduct at Aberdeen to go before a court-martial and was charged with the most rapes.

In a pre-trial motion, lawyers for another Army drill sergeant facing charges of sexual assault and violation of orders said Monday the instructor was singled out by the prosecution because he is an African-American male.
Captain Art Coulter, defence counsel for Staff Sgt. Vernell Robinson Jr., said military regulations applied to the privates who accused him as well as the sergeant.
But, Coulter said, while the accusers also had violated orders, only his client has been charged.

Seven female trainees have accused Robinson of sexual assault, improper sexual relations or sexual harassment between April and September 1996. One male has accused him of wrongful consumption of alcohol with trainees.
Robinson faces a court-martial starting May 27.
Government prosecutors called the defence accusations "absurd" and Judge Paul Johnston has not ruled on the defence motion.
The argument is the first time the defence attorney has raised the race and gender issue in court.
